title: Around the World in Eighty Days: Retold
author: Jules Verne
retoldBy: Retold for Grammar Stream from “Around the World in Eighty Days” by Jules Verne (1873)
blurb: Phileas Fogg bets half his fortune that he can race round the world in eighty days. With his loyal servant Passepartout, and a detective hot on their heels, he crosses the world by steamship, train, elephant and a sledge with sails, right down to the very last second.
note: A retelling of Verne’s novel (serialised in French in 1872, published as a book in 1873) that keeps the wager, the route, the dates, Inspector Fix and the date-line twist. Changes: the attack on the train is made by unnamed robbers, with nobody killed, instead of the original’s stereotyped Sioux raid; Aouda’s rescue is told gently; Verne’s remarks about peoples and religions, the Mormon chapter, Colonel Proctor’s duel and the opium den are left out (Fix uses a sleeping powder); Passepartout leaves the temple in a hurry rather than fighting; the punches become a thump and a push.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Most Exact Man in London
paragraphs: In the year 1872, at Number 7, Savile Row, in London, there lived a gentleman called Mr Phileas Fogg.

Mr Fogg was rich, but nobody knew how he had made his money. He was polite, but he hardly ever spoke. And he was *exact*. Everything he did, he did at precisely the same minute every day. He got up at eight o’clock exactly. He had his tea and toast at twenty-three minutes past eight. At half past eleven exactly he walked to his club, the Reform Club, where he ate his meals, read the newspapers and played a card game called whist. And at midnight exactly he went home to bed.
He was so exact that he never hurried and was never late. He never took one step more than he needed. He was, people said, as regular as a clock.

On the morning of the 2nd of October, Mr Fogg had just sent away his servant, because the poor fellow had brought him shaving water that was two degrees too cold. Now he sat in his armchair, as straight as a soldier, watching a clock that showed the seconds, minutes, hours, days, months and years. He was waiting for his new servant.
There was a knock, and a cheerful young man of about thirty came in and bowed.
“You are French, I believe,” said Mr Fogg, “and your name is John?”

“Jean, if you please, sir,” said the young man. “Jean Passepartout. I have had many jobs. I have been a singer, a circus rider and an acrobat, and a fireman in Paris. But now I want a quiet life. I heard that Mr Phileas Fogg was the most regular gentleman in England, who never travels anywhere, so I have come to you.”
“Passepartout will do,” said Mr Fogg. “What time is it?”
Passepartout pulled out an enormous silver watch. “Twenty-two minutes past eleven.”
“You are four minutes slow,” said Mr Fogg. “No matter. From this moment, twenty-nine minutes past eleven, on Wednesday the 2nd of October, you are in my service.”
And Mr Fogg stood up, put on his hat and went out without another word.
Passepartout explored the house from top to bottom. It was clean and neat and quiet. A card on the wall listed exactly what he had to do at every minute of the day. He rubbed his hands with delight.
“This is just what I wanted!” he said. “Mr Fogg and I will get on very well. He is a real machine. And I don’t mind serving a machine!”
But Passepartout’s quiet life was about to come to a sudden end.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Wager
paragraphs: That afternoon, at the Reform Club, Mr Fogg’s friends were talking about a robbery. Three days before, a thief had walked into the Bank of England and stolen fifty-five thousand pounds in banknotes. The police said he looked like a gentleman. Detectives had been sent to every big port in the world to catch him.
“He’ll never get away,” said Mr Ralph, who worked at the bank. “Where could he go?”
“Oh, the world is big enough,” said Mr Stuart.
“It was once,” said Mr Fogg quietly, from behind his newspaper.
“What do you mean? Has the world grown smaller?”
“In a way, yes,” said Mr Ralph. “With fast trains and steamships, a man can now go round the world in three months.”
“In eighty days,” said Mr Fogg.

It was true. Mr Sullivan read out a list from the newspaper. By train and steamship, it said, you could go from London to Suez in Egypt in seven days, then to Bombay in India in thirteen, across India by train to Calcutta in three, on to Hong Kong in thirteen, to Yokohama in Japan in six, across the Pacific Ocean to San Francisco in twenty-two, across America to New York in seven, and home to London in nine. Eighty days in all.
“But that’s only on paper!” cried Mr Stuart. “What about storms, and shipwrecks, and trains coming off the rails?”
“All included,” said Mr Fogg, calmly playing his cards.
“I’d like to see you do it, then. I’ll bet four thousand pounds it can’t be done!”

“On the contrary, it can,” said Mr Fogg. “I will bet twenty thousand pounds that I can go round the world in eighty days or less. That is one thousand nine hundred and twenty hours, or one hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes. Do you accept?”
His friends looked at each other. Twenty thousand pounds was half of everything Mr Fogg owned! But they agreed.

“Good,” said Mr Fogg. “The train for Dover leaves at a quarter to nine this evening. I will take it. Today is Wednesday the 2nd of October. So I shall be back here, in this very room, on Saturday the 21st of December, at a quarter to nine in the evening. If I am not, my twenty thousand pounds is yours.”
Soon after half past seven, Mr Fogg arrived home, hours earlier than usual.
“Passepartout!” he called. “We leave for Dover in ten minutes. We are going round the world.”
Passepartout’s eyes nearly popped out of his head. “Round the world?” he whispered.
“In eighty days. So we have not a moment to lose. No trunks. Just one carpet bag, with two shirts and three pairs of stockings each. We will buy what we need on the way.”
Passepartout packed in a daze. When he came down, Mr Fogg put a fat roll of banknotes into the bag.
“Take great care of it,” he said. “There are twenty thousand pounds inside.”
Passepartout nearly dropped it.

At the station, a poor woman with a baby in her arms and bare, muddy feet asked them for money. Mr Fogg gave her all the money he had won at cards that afternoon. “Here, my good woman,” he said. “I am glad I met you.” Passepartout felt his eyes go misty. Perhaps his new master had a kind heart after all.
At a quarter to nine the whistle blew, and the train slid out into the dark, rainy night. Suddenly Passepartout gave a cry of horror.
“What is the matter?” asked Mr Fogg.
“In my hurry, I forgot to turn off the gas lamp in my room!”
“Very well,” said Mr Fogg calmly. “It will burn, at your expense.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. A Detective at Suez
paragraphs: Seven days later, a small, nervous man with bright eyes was pacing up and down the quay at Suez, in Egypt, waiting for a steamship called the *Mongolia*. His name was Mr Fix, and he was a detective from London. He was looking for the bank robber, and if he caught him he would win a big reward.

When the *Mongolia* arrived, a cheerful young Frenchman came ashore and asked Fix the way to the British consul’s office, to get his master’s passport stamped. Fix glanced at the passport, and his heart jumped. The description of Phileas Fogg was exactly like the description of the bank robber!
Fix hurried to the consul. “My man is on that ship,” he said.
Soon Mr Fogg himself came in to have his passport stamped. “I wish to prove that I came through Suez,” he said politely, and then he went back to his ship.
“He looks like a perfectly honest man,” said the consul.
“Clever robbers always do,” said Fix.
Then Fix went to make friends with Passepartout, who was buying new shirts and shoes.
“Is this Egypt?” asked Passepartout. “In Africa? Just think! I thought we were only going as far as Paris, and all I saw of Paris was through a train window in the pouring rain!”
He pulled out his big silver watch. “We have plenty of time. It’s only ten to ten.”
“Your watch is slow,” said Fix. “It is twelve o’clock here.”
“My watch? Slow? It was my great-grandfather’s, and it never loses five minutes in a year!”
“You are still on London time,” said Fix. “The sun rises earlier here, because we are further east. You should change your watch in each country.”
“Change my watch? Never!” said Passepartout. “If the sun doesn’t agree with my watch, then the sun is wrong!”

As they walked, Passepartout chattered happily. “My master is going round the world in eighty days,” he said. “He says it is a bet, but I don’t believe it. And he carries an enormous amount of money in brand-new banknotes!”
That was enough for Fix. A rich man who had left London in a great hurry, soon after the robbery, carrying piles of new banknotes, on a silly excuse about a bet? He was sure he had found his thief.

But Fix could not arrest anyone without a warrant, a special paper from the police in London. So he sent a telegram asking for a warrant to be sent to Bombay. Then he grabbed his bag and jumped on board the *Mongolia*, just as it set off down the Red Sea.

The ship steamed on, past hot deserts and blue seas. Mr Fogg played whist in his cabin all day and never once looked out at the view. On the 20th of October they reached Bombay, in India, two whole days ahead of time. Mr Fogg wrote it down in his notebook.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. An Elephant for Two Thousand Pounds
paragraphs: The train for Calcutta did not leave Bombay until eight o’clock, so Passepartout went to look at the city. He saw a wonderful festival with music and dancing, and then a beautiful temple on a hill. He walked straight in to admire it.

But Passepartout did not know that visitors must take off their shoes before entering, to show respect. He was still wearing his! The priests were very upset, and they rushed towards him. In a fright, Passepartout ran out of the temple so fast that he left his shoes behind, and he arrived at the station just in time, without hat or shoes, and quite out of breath.
“I hope this will not happen again,” said Mr Fogg coldly.

Fix, who was watching from a dark corner of the platform, rubbed his hands. “He has broken the law in India,” he thought. “Now I can have them stopped!” And instead of getting on the train, he went to find the priests.

On the train, Mr Fogg met an old whist partner from the ship, a kind army officer called Sir Francis Cromarty, who knew India well. Through the night and the next day they rattled across India, past forests and farms and rivers, while Passepartout gazed out of the window. He did not want to go home any more. He wanted Mr Fogg to win!
Then, in the middle of a forest, the train stopped. “Everybody out!” called the guard. “The railway isn’t finished. There are fifty miles still to build before the line starts again at Allahabad.”
“But the newspapers said it was finished!” cried Sir Francis.
“The newspapers were wrong.”
Sir Francis was furious. But Mr Fogg only said, “I had two days to spare. I will use them. We will find another way.”
They searched the village, but every cart and pony had already been taken by the other passengers. Then Passepartout came running.
“Sir, I have found an elephant!”

The elephant was called Kiouni. He was big and strong and gentle, and he could travel quickly for a long time. But his owner did not want to sell him. Mr Fogg offered to rent him for ten pounds an hour, then twenty, then forty. The owner shook his head. Mr Fogg offered to buy him for a thousand pounds. Still no.
“Mr Fogg,” whispered Sir Francis, “think before you spend any more!”
“I need this elephant,” said Mr Fogg, “and I will have him.” Twelve hundred pounds. Fifteen hundred. Eighteen hundred. Passepartout went quite white.
At two thousand pounds, the owner agreed.
“What a price for an elephant!” groaned Passepartout.

A clever young guide who knew all the forest paths offered to drive the elephant. Mr Fogg and Sir Francis sat in baskets on each side of Kiouni’s back, and Passepartout sat in the middle, bouncing up and down like a ball. He laughed all the way, and fed Kiouni lumps of sugar.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Rescue in the Forest
paragraphs: On the second afternoon, deep in a forest, Kiouni suddenly stopped. Through the trees came the sound of drums and singing. The guide quickly hid the elephant in the bushes.

A long, slow procession passed by, with music and priests in robes. In the middle walked a young woman, covered in jewels. She stumbled at every step, as if she were half asleep. Behind her, men were carrying the body of a very old prince who had died.
When the procession had gone, Sir Francis looked very sad.

“That poor young woman is the old prince’s widow,” he said quietly. “In a very few places, there is still a cruel old custom that a widow must share her husband’s funeral fire. The law has forbidden it, and most people in India think it is a terrible thing. But out here, far from the towns, nobody can stop it.”

“And she has not agreed to it,” said the guide. “Everybody knows her story. Her name is Aouda. She is the daughter of a merchant from Bombay, and she went to school there. When her parents died, she was made to marry this old prince against her will. Now his relatives want her money, and they have given her something to make her sleepy, so that she cannot fight back. At sunrise tomorrow, she will be in terrible danger.”
Mr Fogg was silent for a moment. Then he said, “Suppose we save this woman.”
“Save her, Mr Fogg?” said Sir Francis.
“I still have twelve hours to spare. I can use them for that.”
“Why, you are a man with a heart after all!”
“Sometimes,” said Mr Fogg quietly. “When I have the time.”

The brave guide said at once that he would help. They crept through the woods to the old temple where Aouda was being kept. But guards were standing at every door all night long. At midnight they tried to make a hole in the back wall, loosening the bricks with their pocket knives. But a shout went up inside, and more guards came round to watch the back. It seemed hopeless.
“We must go,” whispered Sir Francis.
“Wait,” said Mr Fogg. “The chance which now seems lost may come at the last moment.”

Meanwhile, Passepartout had climbed a tree. He was thinking hard. “What a crazy idea!” he muttered to himself. “And yet, why not? It may be our only chance.” And he slipped silently away into the dark.

As the sky grew grey, the drums began again. Aouda was led out to the great pile of wood for the old prince’s funeral fire, where his body already lay. Torches were lit, and thick smoke rose up. Mr Fogg was just about to rush forward, when suddenly there was a cry.

Out of the clouds of smoke, a figure rose up. It was the old prince! At least, that is what everybody thought. He climbed down, holding Aouda in his arms, and walked straight through the crowd. Everybody threw themselves on the ground in terror, and nobody dared to look up.
The figure walked right up to Mr Fogg and Sir Francis and said, “Let’s be off!”
It was Passepartout! In the darkness and the smoke, he had crept up beside the funeral fire, wrapped himself in the old prince’s cloak and carried Aouda away.
In a moment they were all on Kiouni’s back, crashing away through the forest as fast as the elephant could go. By the time the crowd realised they had been tricked, the rescuers were far away.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Shoes in Court and a Storm at Sea
paragraphs: Aouda slept for a long time. When she woke up on the train, she could not believe where she was. Sir Francis told her the whole story, and she thanked her rescuers with tears in her eyes.
“You cannot stay in India,” Sir Francis said. “Your husband’s relatives will look for you.”
“Then come with us as far as Hong Kong,” said Mr Fogg. “I believe you have a cousin there.” And Aouda gratefully agreed.

Before they left, Mr Fogg paid the guide what he had promised, and then he said, “You have been brave and faithful. I have paid for your work, but not for your courage. Would you like this elephant? He is yours.”
“Sir, you are giving me a fortune!” cried the guide.
Kiouni lifted Passepartout high in the air with his trunk, and set him gently down again, as if to say goodbye.

At Benares, Sir Francis said goodbye too, and on the 25th of October they reached Calcutta, exactly on time. The ship to Hong Kong left at noon. But as they stepped off the train, a policeman came up.
“Mr Phileas Fogg? Please come with me.”

He took them to a court. The judge put on his wig. (At first he put on his clerk’s wig by mistake, and had to swap.) Then three priests from the temple in Bombay came in to complain. And on the judge’s desk the clerk placed a pair of shoes.
“My shoes!” cried Passepartout, before he could stop himself.
Fix had brought the priests all the way to Calcutta by the fastest train. Because of the rescue in the forest, they had arrived first.
“You went into the temple without taking off your shoes,” said the judge. “That is not allowed. You must go to prison for fifteen days. And Mr Fogg, as your master, must go to prison for a week.”
Fix smiled to himself. A week in Calcutta would give his warrant plenty of time to arrive.

But Mr Fogg stood up. “I offer bail,” he said. Bail is money you pay to the court so that you can go free until your case is finished. The judge asked for a thousand pounds each. Mr Fogg took two thousand pounds out of the carpet bag and put it on the desk.
“Come,” he said to Passepartout.
“At least give me back my shoes!” said Passepartout. “These shoes have cost more than a thousand pounds each, and they pinch my feet!”
An hour later they were on board the steamship *Rangoon*, and Fix was stamping his feet on the quay with rage. “He’s escaped!” he groaned. “I’ll follow him to the end of the world if I have to!”

On board the *Rangoon*, Aouda grew to know Mr Fogg better. He visited her every day at exactly the same time, listened to her politely, and made sure she had everything she needed. He never said much. But Aouda began to think he was the kindest man she had ever met.
One morning, Passepartout found Fix on deck.
“Monsieur Fix! What are you doing here? Are you going round the world too?”
“No, no, only to Hong Kong,” said Fix. “I have been seasick in my cabin.”

Passepartout began to wonder. Why did Mr Fix keep turning up wherever they went? Then he had an idea. “Of course!” he thought. “He is a spy, sent by the gentlemen of the Reform Club to make sure my master really goes round the world! Well, I shall say nothing to Mr Fogg. But I shall tease Mr Fix a little.”
“You are a sly one, Monsieur Fix,” he said with a wink. Fix did not know what to think.

Then a storm blew up. Huge waves rolled the ship from side to side, and the wind roared in the rigging. Passepartout was frantic. Fix was delighted. And Mr Fogg sat calmly in the saloon, as if the storm were part of his plan.
The *Rangoon* reached Hong Kong a whole day late. The ship to Yokohama, in Japan, should have left the day before.
“When does the next ship leave for Yokohama?” Mr Fogg asked the harbour pilot.
“Tomorrow morning, sir. The *Carnatic*. She should have gone yesterday, but she had to mend one of her boilers.”
“Thank you,” said Mr Fogg, as calmly as ever. Passepartout wanted to hug the pilot.
In Hong Kong, Mr Fogg went to look for Aouda’s cousin, but he learned that the cousin had moved to Holland two years before. Aouda did not know what to do.
“It is very simple,” said Mr Fogg. “Come with us to Europe. Passepartout, go and book three cabins on the *Carnatic*.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Passepartout Is Tricked
paragraphs: At the shipping office, Passepartout found that the *Carnatic* would leave that very evening instead of the next morning. He was just going to tell his master when Fix took his arm.
“Come and have a drink with me,” said Fix. “I have something important to tell you.”
They sat down in a café by the harbour. Fix leaned close.

“I am not a spy for the Reform Club,” he said. “I am a police detective.” He showed Passepartout his badge. “A man robbed the Bank of England of fifty-five thousand pounds, and I believe your master is that man. Help me keep him here in Hong Kong for a few days, and I will share the reward with you.”

Passepartout banged the table. “Never!” he cried. “Even if what you say is true, which I don’t believe, Mr Fogg has been good and generous and brave. I will never betray him, not for all the gold in the world!”
“Very well,” said Fix. “Forget I said anything. Finish your drink.”
But while Passepartout was not looking, Fix had slipped a strong sleeping powder into his cup. In a few minutes, Passepartout’s head drooped on to the table, and he was fast asleep.
“At last!” said Fix. “Now Mr Fogg will not hear that the ship is leaving early.” And he crept away.

Passepartout slept for hours. But even in his sleep, one thought kept nagging at him: *the Carnatic, the Carnatic!* At last he woke, staggered out of the café and down to the quay, and stumbled up the gangplank just as the *Carnatic* was moving off. Then he collapsed on the deck, and the sailors carried him to a bunk.
The next morning, Mr Fogg and Aouda went down to the harbour. The *Carnatic* had gone, and so had Passepartout.
“It is an accident, madam,” said Mr Fogg. “Nothing more.”
Fix stepped forward, pretending to be surprised. “The *Carnatic* has gone? How unlucky! Now we must wait a week for the next ship.”
His heart leaped. A week! His warrant would surely arrive. But Mr Fogg only said, “There are other boats in Hong Kong harbour, I think.”
For three hours Mr Fogg searched the docks. At last he found a sailor called John Bunsby, who owned a small, fast pilot boat called the *Tankadere*.

“Yokohama is too far for my little boat,” said Bunsby. “But the big American steamship to San Francisco really starts from Shanghai, in China. It leaves there in four days. If the wind is kind, I can get you to Shanghai in time.”
“Agreed,” said Mr Fogg. “I will pay you a hundred pounds a day, and two hundred more if we arrive in time.” Then he turned politely to Fix. “Would you like to come with us, sir?”
Fix could hardly believe it. He was going to chase Mr Fogg, on Mr Fogg’s boat, at Mr Fogg’s expense!
Before they sailed, Mr Fogg left money with the police and asked them to search for Passepartout. Then the *Tankadere* spread her white sails and flew out to sea.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. A Typhoon and a Long Nose
paragraphs: At first the *Tankadere* skimmed over the waves like a seagull. But on the second day the sky turned dark and strange.
“A typhoon is coming,” said John Bunsby. A typhoon is a huge, whirling storm.
“Is it coming from the north or the south?” asked Mr Fogg.
“From the south.”
“Good. Then it will blow us the way we are going.”

All day and all night the little boat was thrown about by mountainous waves. Aouda was very brave, and Mr Fogg stayed beside her to protect her from the spray. When the storm was over, they were still a hundred miles from Shanghai, and there was only one day left.

At seven o’clock on the last evening, they were still three miles from Shanghai. And there, in the distance, a long black funnel puffing smoke appeared on the edge of the sea. It was the American steamship, leaving without them!
“Signal her!” said Mr Fogg.

They raised their flag halfway up the mast, which is the signal for a ship in trouble, and fired the little brass cannon on the deck. *Boom!* The steamship turned towards them. Mr Fogg, Aouda and Fix climbed aboard, and Mr Fogg paid John Bunsby a very handsome reward.

Meanwhile, Passepartout had woken up on the *Carnatic*, far out at sea. He searched the ship for his master, but Mr Fogg was not on board. “It’s all my fault!” he groaned, tugging his hair. “I forgot to tell him the ship was leaving early. And that wicked Fix tricked me!”

When he reached Yokohama, Passepartout had no money at all, not even a penny. He swapped his smart clothes for an old Japanese coat and a few coins, and bought himself some rice. Then he saw a man carrying a big poster.
ACROBATIC TROUPE! LAST SHOWS BEFORE LEAVING FOR AMERICA! THE LONG NOSES!
“America! That’s just what I want!” said Passepartout.
The troupe belonged to an American showman called Mr Batulcar. “Can you sing standing on your head, with a top spinning on one foot?” he asked.
“I think so,” said Passepartout, remembering his circus days. And so he got the job.

The show was amazing. Jugglers kept dozens of tops spinning along strings and the edges of fans. Acrobats tumbled and leapt. And best of all were the Long Noses: acrobats in costumes with wings, wearing enormous noses made of bamboo, five, six or even ten feet long. They balanced on each other’s noses and somersaulted from one nose to the next.

For the grand finale they built a human pyramid, standing on top of each other’s noses, higher and higher, right up to the roof. Passepartout lay on his back at the very bottom, wearing wings and a nose six feet long, holding up the whole tower.
Suddenly he saw somebody in the audience. He leaped up, the whole pyramid came tumbling down like a house of cards, and Passepartout scrambled into the crowd crying, “Oh, my master! My master!”
“You here?” said Mr Fogg.
“Myself!”
“Very well. Then let us go to the steamship, young man.”
So Passepartout went aboard the ship to San Francisco still wearing his wings and his six-foot nose.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. Across America
paragraphs: The great paddle steamer *General Grant* churned across the wide Pacific Ocean. One day, Passepartout pulled out his great-grandfather’s watch and gave a shout of triumph. His watch said nine o’clock, and the ship’s clock said nine o’clock too!
“You see?” he cried. “I never changed my watch, and now the sun has come round to agree with it!”

Poor Passepartout did not know the truth. Out here on the ship, halfway round the world, it was nine o’clock in the *morning*. But his watch still showed London time, and in London it was nine o’clock at *night*. His watch could not tell the difference. And he certainly did not know how much that would matter at the very end of the journey.
Think about it: Passepartout’s watch has only twelve hours on its face. Why can’t it tell the difference between nine in the morning and nine at night? Remember this. It will matter later!

Fix was on board too. He had found his warrant waiting at last in Yokohama, but it was no use outside British land. So he had decided to follow Mr Fogg all the way home to England, and arrest him there.
When Passepartout saw Fix on deck, he marched straight up to him and gave him such a thump that the detective sat down hard on the deck, with his hat over his eyes.
“Have you finished?” asked Fix, getting up.
“For now,” said Passepartout.

“Then listen. Until now I have tried to keep your master back. But from now on, I want him to get to England as fast as possible, so that I can arrest him there. So I will help you. Shall we work together?”
“Friends? No,” said Passepartout. “But partners, perhaps. And if you play any more tricks, I’ll twist your neck!”

They reached San Francisco on the 3rd of December, neither early nor late. While they waited for the train, they got caught in a huge, noisy crowd shouting about an election. A big man with a red beard swung his fist at Mr Fogg, but Fix jumped in the way and took the blow himself. Mr Fogg thanked him. He had no idea that Fix wanted to arrest him!

That evening they boarded the great train that runs all the way across America. It had beds that folded out of the walls at night, and they rattled through snowy mountains and over wide, empty plains.
One day the train had to stop for three hours while an enormous herd of buffaloes, thousands and thousands of them, crossed the track in front of it. Passepartout fumed. Mr Fogg waited calmly.
Then, high in the mountains, a signalman stopped the train. “You can’t go on!” he said. “The bridge at Medicine Bow is cracked and shaky. It won’t hold the weight of the train.”
“Perhaps there is a way,” said the driver. “If we go at top speed, we might just get over before it falls.”
“It would be more sensible for us all to walk across, and let the train come after,” said Passepartout. But nobody listened to him.

The driver reversed the train for nearly a mile, like a long jumper taking a run-up. Then, with a scream of the whistle, it raced forward, faster and faster, until it hardly seemed to touch the rails. It flew across the bridge in a flash, and just as the last carriage reached the other side, the whole bridge crashed down into the rushing river behind them!

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Robbers, a Rescue and a Sledge with Sails
paragraphs: A few days later, as the train rushed across the snowy plains, there was a sudden terrible noise. A gang of train robbers had leapt on board! They knocked out the driver and his fireman, and one of them, trying to stop the engine, pulled the wrong lever. Instead of slowing down, the train raced faster and faster.
The passengers fought back bravely. But the train had to be stopped before it passed the next station, Fort Kearney, where there were soldiers who could help.
“I will go,” said Passepartout.

Using all his old acrobat’s skills, he slipped out of a door, swung himself underneath the carriage and crawled along under the rushing train, from carriage to carriage, holding on to chains and bars, until he reached the very front. There, hanging on with one hand, he loosened the heavy coupling that joined the carriages to the engine. With a jolt it came free! The engine roared away by itself, and the carriages rolled slower and slower, until they stopped right beside Fort Kearney.
Soldiers came running, and the robbers fled. But when the passengers counted each other, three were missing. One of them was Passepartout! The robbers had carried him off.
Mr Fogg folded his arms. If he went to rescue Passepartout, he would certainly miss his train, and probably lose his bet. Aouda looked at him, and he understood her look.
“I will find him,” he said.

The captain of the fort did not want to send his soldiers. “Then I will go alone,” said Mr Fogg. That made the captain change his mind. “No, sir, you are a brave man,” he said. “Thirty volunteers!” Every soldier stepped forward.
Mr Fogg asked Fix to stay with Aouda, and he set off across the snow with the soldiers.

All that day and all that night Aouda waited, watching the white plains. At last the runaway engine came puffing back, and the train went on its way without them. Fix stayed, sitting silently on a bench. At dawn, there was a shout. Mr Fogg was marching back across the snow, with Passepartout and the two other passengers safe beside him. They had found the robbers’ camp, and just as they arrived, Passepartout had been fighting his captors with his fists!
“I must say,” said Passepartout, “I cost my master a great deal!”
But the train had gone. Mr Fogg was twenty hours behind time.
Then Fix spoke. “Mr Fogg, there is a man here with a sledge that has sails. With a good wind, it can fly across the snow as fast as a train.”

It was true. The sledge had a tall mast and great white sails. With a strong wind behind it, it skimmed over the frozen plains at forty miles an hour. They huddled together under rugs. The wind sang in the ropes. Once a pack of hungry wolves chased after them, but the sledge soon left them far behind. By lunchtime they had reached Omaha, where they jumped straight on to a train for Chicago, and then another for New York.
At a quarter past eleven on the night of the 11th of December, they ran on to the pier in New York.
The ship to Liverpool had left forty-five minutes before.

chapters.title: Chapter 11. The Ship That Burned Itself
paragraphs: The next morning, Mr Fogg searched the harbour for another ship. At last he found a trading steamer called the *Henrietta*, ready to sail. Her captain, Andrew Speedy, was a grumpy man with red hair and a growling voice.
“Will you take me and three others to Liverpool?” asked Mr Fogg.
“No. I’m going to Bordeaux, in France. And I don’t like passengers.”
“I will pay you two thousand dollars each to take us to Bordeaux.”
The captain scratched his head. Eight thousand dollars! “We leave at nine,” he said.

But Mr Fogg did not really want to go to France. During the first day and night at sea, he paid the sailors so well that they all agreed to follow *his* orders instead. So Captain Speedy found himself locked in his own cabin, roaring with rage, while Mr Fogg steered the *Henrietta* towards Liverpool!
Then there was a new problem. The engineer came to Mr Fogg. “We are burning coal fast to go at full speed,” he said. “We haven’t enough to reach Liverpool.”
“Keep the fires burning anyway,” said Mr Fogg.
When the coal was nearly gone, he sent for Captain Speedy. The captain burst on deck like a bomb going off.
“Pirate!” he yelled.
“I have sent for you, sir,” said Mr Fogg calmly, “to ask you to sell me your ship. I shall have to burn her.”
“Burn the *Henrietta*? She’s worth fifty thousand dollars!”
“Here are sixty thousand.”
The captain’s anger vanished in an instant. “And I keep the iron hull and the engine?”
“The hull and the engine.”
“Agreed!”

So Mr Fogg ordered the crew to burn every wooden part of the ship in the furnaces, to keep the engines going. They burned the cabins and the bunks. They burned the masts and the spare planks. They burned the railings and most of the deck. Passepartout chopped and sawed away with all his might. By the end, the *Henrietta* was just a flat iron shell, puffing along on the last of her wood.

They reached Ireland, and Mr Fogg had another clever idea. Instead of going on to Liverpool, he stopped at the port of Queenstown. From there, a fast train took them to Dublin, and a fast boat took them across the sea to Liverpool. At twenty minutes to twelve, on what Mr Fogg’s notebook said was the eightieth and last day, they stepped ashore in England. London was only six hours away.
At that very moment, Fix put his hand on Mr Fogg’s shoulder.
“Phileas Fogg,” he said, “I arrest you in the Queen’s name!”
Mr Fogg was locked up in a room in the Custom House. Passepartout was in despair. Aouda wept. Mr Fogg sat calmly on a wooden bench and put his watch on the table, watching the minutes tick away.
At half past two, the door burst open. In rushed Passepartout, Aouda and Fix, who was so out of breath he could hardly speak.
“Sir!” he gasped. “Forgive me! A terrible mistake! The real robber was caught three days ago! You are free!”
Mr Fogg looked at Fix. Then, with the only quick movement he had ever made in his whole life, he gave the detective such a push that Fix sat down hard on the floor.
“Well done!” cried Passepartout.

There was no time to lose. Mr Fogg hired a special train all to himself and raced towards London. But there were delays along the line, and when he stepped down on to the platform in London, all the clocks showed ten minutes to nine.
He was five minutes late. He had lost the wager.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. “Here I Am, Gentlemen!”
paragraphs: Mr Fogg went quietly home to Savile Row. The first thing Passepartout did was to turn off the gas lamp in his room, which had been burning for eighty days.

Mr Fogg was ruined. He had spent almost all the money in the carpet bag on the journey, and now he would have to give his last twenty thousand pounds to his friends at the club. But he did not blame anybody.
“It was all my fault!” cried Passepartout.
“I blame no one,” said Mr Fogg.
The next evening, he went to talk to Aouda.
“Madam,” he said, “will you forgive me for bringing you to England? When I decided to take you far away from danger, I was rich, and I meant to give you part of my fortune. Now I am poor.”
“Mr Fogg,” said Aouda, taking his hand, “I don’t want your fortune. They say that troubles shared by two people who care about each other are easier to bear. Will you have me for your wife?”
Mr Fogg stood up. For the first time ever, there was a light in his eyes, and his lips trembled. “I love you!” he said simply. “Yes, I love you, and I am entirely yours!”
Passepartout’s round face beamed like the sun. He was sent at once to ask the vicar, the Reverend Samuel Wilson, to marry them the next day, Monday. Off he ran.
But half an hour later he came racing back, with his hair wild and his hat gone, so out of breath he could hardly speak.
“Master!” he gasped. “The wedding! Impossible! Not tomorrow!”
“Why not?”
“Because tomorrow is Sunday!”
“Monday,” said Mr Fogg.
“No! Today is *Saturday*! You have made a mistake of one whole day! We arrived twenty-four hours early! But there are only ten minutes left!”
Passepartout grabbed his master by the collar and dragged him out of the house. Mr Fogg leaped into a cab and promised the driver a hundred pounds. They galloped through the streets of London.
At the Reform Club, Mr Fogg’s five friends were watching the clock. A great crowd waited outside.
“Twenty minutes to nine,” said Mr Stuart. “In five minutes, we shall have won.”
“Seventeen minutes to nine…”
“Sixteen minutes to nine…”

They counted the seconds. Forty seconds… fifty… fifty-five… A great cheer rose up from the street outside. Fifty-seven… The door flew open, and before the clock could tick the sixtieth second, there stood Phileas Fogg.
“Here I am, gentlemen!” he said calmly.
He had done it! He had gone round the world in eighty days, and won his wager!
But how could the most exact man in London have made a mistake of a whole day?

Here is the answer. Mr Fogg had travelled all the way round the world going *east*, towards the sunrise. Every time he travelled a long way east, the sun came up a little earlier for him. So each of his days was a little bit shorter than a day in London: on average, about eighteen minutes shorter. Day by day, all those little bits of time added up. Eighty days of eighteen minutes makes one thousand four hundred and forty minutes, and that is exactly twenty-four hours: one whole day!

So Mr Fogg had counted eighty sunrises on his journey. But back in London, only seventy-nine sunrises had happened. So when he stepped off the train in London, he thought it was Saturday evening and that he was five minutes late. But it was really Friday evening, and he was a whole day early! And if Passepartout’s watch had shown the date as well as the hours, it would have told him so.

Today, there is an imaginary line in the middle of the Pacific Ocean called the *date line*. When travellers cross it going east, they count the same day twice, so that their calendar comes out right. But Mr Fogg never did that, and so he gained a day without knowing it.

Mr Fogg had spent nearly nineteen thousand pounds on the journey, so he did not end up much richer. He shared the thousand pounds that was left between Passepartout and Fix. But first, being exact, he took away from Passepartout’s share the cost of the gas that had burned in his room for one thousand nine hundred and twenty hours.
Two days later, Mr Fogg and Aouda were married, and Passepartout, dazzling in his best clothes, walked proudly beside the bride.
The next morning, Passepartout knocked excitedly on his master’s door.
“Sir! I have just worked out that we could have gone round the world in only seventy-eight days!”
“No doubt,” said Mr Fogg, “if we had not crossed India. But if I had not crossed India, I should not have saved Aouda, she would not be my wife, and…” And Mr Fogg quietly closed the door.

So what did Phileas Fogg bring back from his journey round the world? Nothing, you might say. Nothing except a wife he loved, and a friend who would follow him anywhere. And wouldn’t you go round the world for less than that?
